title: More Than Just Data
body:
My Journey into Analytics
My journey into data analytics has been one of continuous learning, curiosity, and discovery. What started with an academic foundation in Geoinformatics gradually evolved into a deeper interest in understanding data, uncovering patterns, and turning information into meaningful insights.

Over time, I've come to realize that working with data is about much more than writing queries, building dashboards, or automating processes. It's about asking the right questions, understanding the problem behind the numbers, and finding ways to make information useful.

Throughout my journey, I've learned a few lessons that continue to shape the way I approach my work:

Curiosity is essential. Never be afraid to ask why something looks the way it does. Sometimes the most valuable insights come from questioning what others take for granted.

There is always more than one way to solve a problem. The first solution isn't necessarily the best one. Exploring alternatives often leads to more efficient and sustainable approaches.

Understand the data before analysing it. A beautiful dashboard means very little if the underlying data isn't reliable or the business context isn't understood.

Never stop learning. Technology evolves, tools change, and new challenges emerge. Staying curious and adaptable is part of becoming a better analyst.

Don't underestimate the basics. Some of the most effective solutions aren't necessarily the most complicated ones.

One thing I've particularly come to appreciate is that growth doesn't always happen through major projects or significant milestones. Sometimes it's found in debugging a stubborn piece of code, simplifying a complicated process, or discovering a better way to approach an everyday task.

I'm still learning, still experimenting, and still finding new ways to approach problems. If there's one thing this journey has taught me, it's that becoming a better data analyst is less about knowing everything and more about being willing to learn something new every day.

And this is only the beginning.

title: Five SQL habits that save me time
body:
None of these are clever. They just make a query easier to read six weeks later.

## Name the grain

Before writing a join, say in a comment what one row of the result represents. Most wrong totals come from a join that quietly changed the grain.

```
-- one row per placement per week
SELECT placement_id, week_start, SUM(units) AS units
FROM   sales
GROUP  BY placement_id, week_start;
```

Then count rows before and after each join. If the number moves when it should not, you found the problem early.
